> ६-३-५३ । इति पादस्य पद्भावः । यद्वा । तत्र साधुरिति यत् । यतोऽनाथ इत्याद्युदात्तत्वं । त्र्यविं । अव रक्षणादिसु । इन्नितीन्प्रत्ययः । कृत्सरः । रेरिहाणा । लिह
> आस्वादन इत्यस्य यज्‌लुकि शानचि रूपं । अभ्यस्तस्वरः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

(Continuing) Or "trayavi" because he protects the three worlds, pervading them with his own splendour. Licking (rerihāṇā), she stands. Knowing the seat, the abode, of ṛta, that is, of Āditya who is truth, I move about: I serve that Āditya with oblations.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- पद्मा (*padmā*)—the earth **NOTE**
- पुरुरूपा (*pururūpā*)—of manifold forms
- वपूंषि (*vapūṃṣi*)—forms of the nature of the unmoving and the moving
- वस्ते (*vaste*)—she wears
- ऊर्ध्वा (*ūrdhvā*)—from a high place in the form of the northern altar
- त्रैविं (*traiviṃ*)—Āditya, who is like a son of one and a half years **NOTE**
- रेरिहाणा (*rerihāṇā*)—licking by means of the oblation
- तस्थौ (*tasthau*)—she stands
- यतस्य (*yatasya*)—of Āditya, who is of the nature of truth **NOTE**
- सद्म (*sadma*)—the abode
- विद्वान् (*vidvān*)—I who know
- वि चरामि (*vi carāmi*)—I worship him
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods
- असुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ*)—the might
- महत् (*mahat*)—is great
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—and without a second

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The earth wears forms of many kinds, of the nature of the unmoving and the moving. From a high place in the form of the northern altar she stands licking, by means of the oblation, Āditya, who is like a son of one and a half years. I, who know the abode of Āditya, who is of the nature of truth, worship him with oblations. The might of the gods is great and without a second.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
The earth wears bodies of many forms : she abides on high cherishing her year and a half old (calf) : knowing the abode of the truth (the sun), I offer worship : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In this Ṛk the earth, जगत्प्रष्टुः परमेश्वरस्य पद्भ्यां जातत्वात् (*jagatpraṣṭuḥ parameśvarasya padbhyāṃ jātatvāt*), since she was born from the feet of the Supreme Lord who made the whole universe, is designated by the word padyā. On this point the mantra is also cited: पद्भ्यां भूमि (*padbhyāṃ bhūmi*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-90-14). Or else, पादसंचारे साधुः (*pādasaṃcāre sādhuḥ*): because she has made for all living beings a way fit for moving about on their own feet, the word padyā is used in the sense of the earth.

### Printed p. 305

For the things born of her, this earth, पुरुरूपा वपूंषि वस्ते (*pururūpā vapūṃṣi vaste*), makes bodies furnished with manifold forms, fixed or moving, and covers their true nature.

त्रैविं—सार्थसंवत्सरवयस्कः वत्सः (*traiviṃ—sārthasaṃvatsaravayaskaḥ vatsaḥ*): the meaning is given as a calf one and a half years old. Or त्री लोकान् अवति स्वतेजसा व्याप्न्नोति (*trī lokān avati svatejasā vyāpnnoti*): he is explained as the one who pervades and protects the three worlds with his splendour.

ऊर्ध्वा—उत्तरवेदात्मना उन्नता । (*ūrdhvā—uttaravedātmanā unnatā |*) This earth is described as standing high in the sacrificial hall in the form of the northern altar, and as satisfying, with the oblations (by the offering of the oblation), Āditya, denoted by the word travi, who is of the measure of a calf of one and a half years.

The sacrificer, who knows the true nature of this Āditya and the dwelling-place where he abides, offers oblations to Āditya; and the might of the gods is described as unequalled and full of greatness.

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> पदे इव । पद्येते ज्ञायेते तत्तदसाधारणलिंगेनेति पदे । अहश्च रात्रिश्चेत्येते दस्मे सर्वैर्दर्शनीये ते उभे अंतर्नभसि मध्ये निहिते स्थापिते इव
> वर्तेते । तयोरहोरात्रयोरन्यद्रात्रिलक्षणं गुह्यमप्रकाशमानतॆया गूढमि-

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

"Padye iva": the two are known (padyete) by their respective distinctive marks, hence "pade". Day and night, these two, "dasme", visible to all, stand, as it were, placed (nihite) within the sky, in the middle. Of the two, day and night, the other, that of the nature of night, is "guhya": hidden, because it does not shine… (the block breaks off here).

### Printed p. 306

> वास्ते । अन्यदहराविः सूर्यप्रकाशेन प्रकटं भवति । सध्रीचीनाहोरात्रयोः
> परस्परमेलनरूपा पथ्या मार्गः । काल इत्यर्थः । सा विषूची । पुण्यकृतोऽपुण्यकृतश्च प्राप्नोतीति विषूची भवति । सर्वे जना अहोरात्रयोर्वर्तंते । यद्वा ।
> पदे इव देवमनुष्यादीनां स्थानभूते द्यावापृथिव्यावंतरंतरिक्षे निहिते वर्तेते ।
> तयोरन्यद्दौर्गुह्यमस्माभिरदृश्यमानतया गूढं वर्तते । अन्यत्पृथिव्याविः सर्वैर्दृश्यमानत्वेन प्रकटा भवति । सध्रीचीनेति पूर्ववत् ॥ सध्रीचीना । सहपूर्वादंचतेः क्विन् । सहस्य सध्रिरिति सध्र्या देशः । विभाषांचेरदिक्स्त्रियामिति खः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa continues his explanation of the preceding verse. The other of the two, the day, becomes manifest through the light of the sun. सध्रीचीना (*sadhrīcīnā*) is the path (पथ्या (*pathyā*)) formed by the day and night meeting each other, that is, time. That path is विषूची (*viṣūcī*): it reaches the doers of merit and the doers of demerit alike. All people live within day and night.

Alternatively, the two पदे इव (*pade iva*) are heaven and earth, the abodes of gods, men and others, which lie placed within the atmosphere. Of these two, one is hidden because we cannot see it; the other, the earth, is manifest because it is seen by all. सध्रीचीना (*sadhrīcīnā*) and the rest are as before.

(The rest of the block is grammar.)

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- दस्मे (*dasme*)—visible to all
- पदे इव (*pade iva*)—the day and the night, both
- अंतः (*aṃtaḥ*)—in the midst of the atmosphere
- निहिते (*nihite*)—are placed
- तयोः (*tayoḥ*)—of those two
- अन्यत् (*anyat*)—the night
- गुह्यं (*guhyaṃ*)—is hidden
- अन्यत् (*anyat*)—the other one, the day
- आविः (*āviḥ*)—is manifest
- सध्रीचीना (*sadhrīcīnā*)—joined together with both of these
- सा पथ्या (*sā pathyā*)—the path in the form of time
- विसूची (*visūcī*)—is common to the whole universe
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods
- असुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ*)—the might
- महत् (*mahat*)—is great
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—and unequalled

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Day and night, both visible to all, are placed in the middle region of the atmosphere. Of the two, the night is hidden and the day is manifest. The path in the form of time, which is joined to both of them together, is common to the whole universe. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Like two (distinguishing) impressions, they (day and night) are placed visible in the midst (between heaven and earth), one hidden, one manifest : the path (of both) is common, and that is universal (for good and evil): great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

अहश्च रात्रिश्चेत्येते सर्वैः दर्शनीये तत्तदसाधारणलिंगेन ज्ञायमाने नभसि मध्यॆ स्थापिते इव वर्तेते । (*ahaśca rātriścetyete sarvaiḥ darśanīye tattadasādhāraṇaliṃgena jñāyamāne nabhasi madhyè sthāpite iva vartete |*). The qualities that belong to day and to night, and their respective marks, are known by everyone as distinguishing them from each other. Since these day-and-nights are endowed with a charming form, they appear as if placed within the atmosphere. They are described as follows: the path that is favourable to both is time; this time is विषूची (*viṣūcī*), that is, पुण्यकृतो अपुण्यकृतश्च प्राप्नोति (*puṇyakṛto apuṇyakṛtaśca prāpnoti*), it pervades all, the virtuous and the sinful alike; and सर्वे जना अहोरात्रयोर्वर्तंते (*sarve janā ahorātrayorvartaṃte*), it provides all living beings with room to live.

### Printed p. 307

The second meaning concerns heaven and earth. यद्वा पदे इव देवमनुष्यादीनां स्थानभूते द्यावापृथिव्य अंतरंतरिक्षे निहिते वर्तते । तयोरन्यत् अन्या द्यौः गुह्यमस्माभिः अदृश्यमानतॆया गूढा वर्तते । अन्या पृथिवी आविः सर्वैः दृश्यमानतेन प्रकटा भवति । (*yadvā pade iva devamanuṣyādīnāṃ sthānabhūte dyāvāpṛthivya aṃtaraṃtarikṣe nihite vartate | tayoranyat anyā dyauḥ guhyamasmābhiḥ adṛśyamānatèyā gūḍhā vartate | anyā pṛthivī āviḥ sarvaiḥ dṛśyamānatena prakaṭā bhavati |*). सध्रीचीनेत्यादि पूर्ववत् (*sadhrīcīnetyādi pūrvavat*). Heaven and earth, which are like dwelling places of gods and men, lie in the atmosphere. Of these, the world of heaven is hidden in a way unknown to us, so that it cannot be seen by us, just as the night is hidden among day and night. The earth is manifest in a form that is known to all, as the day is bright with the light of the sun. Since the time that corresponds to the mutual adherence of these two is the same for the virtuous and the sinful, it is uneven. Because heaven and earth give room to all beings to live, they are benefactors of all; and the might of the gods is described as extraordinary and pre-eminent.

> धेनवो वृष्टिद्वारा सर्वस्य जगतः प्रीणयित्र्योऽशिश्वीः शिशुरहिताः । यद्वा ।
> शिकवो न भवंतीत्यशिश्वीः । शशया नभसि शयाना वर्तमानाः केनाप्यप्रमग्ता अक्षीण-

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The धेनवः (*dhenavaḥ*) are the cows that gratify the whole world by means of rain. अशिश्वीः (*aśiśvīḥ*) means "without young"; or else, शिकवो न भवंतीत्यशिश्वीः (*śikavo na bhavaṃtītyaśiśvīḥ*), "they are not infants". शशयाः (*śaśayāḥ*) are those lying in the sky, unharmed by anyone and undiminished in sap (the sentence continues on the next page).

### Printed p. 308

> रसाः सबर्दुघा उदकलक्षणस्य क्षीरस्य दोग्धो युवतयः परस्परमिश्रणोपेता
> नव्या नव्या अतिशयेन नूतना भवंतीर्दिशो मेघा ना आ धुनयंतां । आदुहंतु ।
> मेघपक्षेशिश्वीर्भवंतीत्यत्र लिंगव्यत्ययः ॥ धुनयंतां । धूञ् कंपने । णिचि
> धूञ् प्रीणोर्नुग्वक्तव्यः । पा- ७-३-३७-१ । इति नुक् । ह्रस्वश्चांदसः । अशिश्वीं । सख्यशिश्वीति भाषायामिति व्यत्ययेन छंदसि भवति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

सबर्दुघाः (*sabardughāḥ*) are those that yield the milk that has the form of water. युवतयः (*yuvatayaḥ*) are those endowed with mutual mixing. The quarters, or the clouds, becoming exceedingly new, नव्या नव्या (*navyā navyā*), are to be shaken, आ धुनयंतां (*ā dhunayaṃtāṃ*), that is, आदुहंतु (*āduhaṃtu*), "let them milk out". In the case of the clouds, in "aśiśvīr bhavanti" there is an exchange of gender. (The rest of the block is grammar.)

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- धेनवः (*dhenavaḥ*)—the cows that gratify the world
- अशिश्वीः (*aśiśvīḥ*)—those without young
- शशयाः (*śaśayāḥ*)—those that remain fixed in the atmosphere
- अप्रदुग्धाः (*apradugdhāḥ*)—those full of sap
- सबर्दुघाः (*sabardughāḥ*)—those that pour out the milk that has the form of water
- युवतयः (*yuvatayaḥ*)—those that are mutually joined
- नव्यानव्याः (*navyānavyāḥ*)—those that always attain newness
- भवंतीः (*bhavaṃtīḥ*)—being so, the clouds (or the quarters)
- आ धुनयंतां (*ā dhunayaṃtāṃ*)—let them be shaken (for the sake of each one)
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods
- असुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ*)—the might
- महत् (*mahat*)—is great
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—and unequalled

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Let the clouds, which gratify the world, are without young, abide fixed in the atmosphere, are full of sap, pour out the milk that has the form of water, are mutually joined and always attain newness, be shaken, each for its own purpose. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
May the milch cows without their young, abiding (in the heaven), and though unmilked, yet yielding milk, and ever fresh and youthful, be shaken (so as to perform their functions) : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

The Anukramaṇikā says that this sixteenth mantra of the sūkta has the quarters (दिग्वचनतॆ (*digvacanatè*)) as its deity. In the bhāṣya Sāyaṇa explains the meaning thus: दिशः मेघा वा आ धुनयंतां आ दुहंतु (*diśaḥ meghā vā ā dhunayaṃtāṃ ā duhaṃtu*), "let the quarters or the clouds keep us in joy". Neither a word for the quarters nor a word for the clouds is used here separately; only the epithets are common to both kinds of meaning, clouds or quarters. The clouds gratify the world by pouring rain. "Aśiśvī" means being without sons, or not having children; शशयाः (*śaśayāḥ*) means remaining in the atmosphere itself;

### Printed p. 309

अप्रदुग्दाः (*apradugdāḥ*) means being filled with water; सबर्दुघाः (*sabardughāḥ*) means milking the milk that has the form of water; युवतयः (*yuvatayaḥ*) means being joined together mutually; नव्यानव्याः (*navyānavyāḥ*) means being in an ever-new manner. Since all these qualities belong to the quarters as well, the prayer of the sacrificer is stated: let these clouds, or these quarters, keep us, the sacrificers, in joy.

#### Ṛk 17

> राजा हि । तत्तत्कर्मानुरूपफलप्रदानेन सर्वेषां राजा खलु ॥ रोरवीति । रु शब्द

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The bull, the rainer of waters, is Indra in the form of Parjanya. When he roars loudly among the other quarters by means of the clouds, that same Parjanya-Indra deposits रेतः (*retaḥ*), water, in another herd, the multitude of the quarters; there it rains. In the world a bull makes a roar over certain cows in order to shed seed, and sheds seed in another herd of cows; it is like that. That Indra is क्षपावान् (*kṣapāvān*): क्षिपति शत्रूनुदकं वेति (*kṣipati śatrūnudakaṃ veti*), he throws enemies or water, so he is possessed of throwing. Or else क्षपा (*kṣapā*) is night: the night that forms a part of the hymns of the rātri-paryāya sacrifices is called so, and he possesses it. He is भगः (*bhagaḥ*), to be worshipped by all. He is the king, for by granting fruit in accordance with each deed he is king of all. (The rest of the block is grammar.)

- यत् (*yat*)—the Indra, of the nature of Parjanya, who
- अन्यासु (*anyāsu*)—in the other quarters
- गोरवीति (*goravīti*)—makes a sound by means of the cloud **NOTE**
- सः (*saḥ*)—that same Indra of the nature of Parjanya

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Indra, the maker of rain and of the nature of Parjanya, makes the sound of thunder in one quarter by means of the cloud and pours down rain in another quarter. Indra is possessed of night, venerable and the lord. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
When the showerer roars in other (regions) he sends down the rain upon a different herd, for he is the victor, the asuspicious, the sovereign : great and unequalled is the might of the gods,

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

The word रेतः (*retaḥ*) is listed among the names of water (Ni. 2-24). Indra, who is in the form of Parjanya, is described as being in the form of a bull. वृषभः अपां वर्षकं अन्यासु दिक्षु मेघद्वारा भृशं शब्दं करोति अन्यस्मि यूथे दितां वृंदे उदकं वर्षति । लोके हि वृषभः कासुचित् गोषु रेतस्सेकार्थं रवं करोति अन्यस्मिन् गोयूथे रेतस्सिंचति तद्वत् । (*vṛṣabhaḥ apāṃ varṣakaṃ anyāsu dikṣu meghadvārā bhṛśaṃ śabdaṃ karoti anyasmi yūthe ditāṃ vṛṃde udakaṃ varṣati | loke hi vṛṣabhaḥ kāsucit goṣu retassekārthaṃ ravaṃ karoti anyasmin goyūthe retassiṃcati tadvat |*) **NOTE**. In the world a bull, while bellowing in a herd of cows, unites with a cow in another herd. In the same way Indra, making a sound through the clouds in order to pour rain in one quarter, pours water in the form of rain in another quarter; thus the likeness to a bull is established for Indra.

Two kinds of meaning are set out for the word क्षपावान् (*kṣapāvān*) **NOTE**. For the word क्षपा (*kṣapā*) the meaning "throwing, hurling" (क्षेपण (*kṣepaṇa*)) is given. From this it is explained that Indra is one who drives away enemies, or one who pours waters down for the worlds.

The word क्षपा (*kṣapā*) is listed among the names of night (Ni. 2-18). Sāyaṇa says क्षपा रात्रिः । रात्रि पर्याययागानां स्तोत्राणां भागभूता या रात्रिः सोच्यते । तद्वान् । (*kṣapā rātriḥ | rātri paryāyayāgānāṃ stotrāṇāṃ bhāgabhūtā yā rātriḥ socyate | tadvān |*). By the word क्षपा (*kṣapā*) night is meant. In the sacrifices performed at night, the nights suitable for reciting hymns contain hymns of Indra; therefore Indra is possessed of क्षपा (*kṣapā*). Thus the second meaning is explained.

सः भगः राजा हि—सर्वैः भजनीयः । तत्तत्कर्मानुपफलप्रदनेन सर्वेषां राजा। (*saḥ bhagaḥ rājā hi—sarvaiḥ bhajanīyaḥ | tattatkarmānupaphalapradanena sarveṣāṃ rājā|*). Indra is one worthy of being served by all, and gives to each the fruit corresponding to his respective deeds; therefore he is the lord. And the might of the gods is described as extraordinary and pre-eminent.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

"O people, let us quickly proclaim the good-horsedness (स्वश्वं (*svaśvaṃ*)) of the hero, the brave Indra, that is, his being possessed of fine horses; and the gods too know his good-horsedness." What is that good-horsedness? It is explained: षोळ्हा (*ṣoḷhā*), at the time of the pairing of the months, the seasons seen as sixfold are represented as horses. Those seasons, six in number, with Hemanta and Śiśira taken together, are yoked five and five and carry Indra, who is of the nature of time. This is Indra's good-horsedness, that he is carried by the seasons. (The rest of the block is grammar.)

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- जनासः (*janāsaḥ*)—O people
- वीरस्य (*vīrasya*)—of the brave Indra
- स्वश्वं (*svaśvaṃ*)—the being accompanied by horses
- नु (*nu*)—right now
- प्र वोचाम (*pra vocāma*)—we proclaim and praise
- देवाः (*devāḥ*)—the gods also
- अस्य (*asya*)—this Indra's being yoked with horses
- नु (*nu*)—at once
- विदुः (*viduḥ*)—know
- षोळ्हा (*ṣoḷhā*)—the horses in the form of the six seasons
- पंचपंचयुक्ताः (*paṃcapaṃcayuktāḥ*)—(Hemanta and Śiśira being undivided) five

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- आ वहंति (*ā vahaṃti*)—carry Indra
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods
- असुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ*)—the might
- महत् (*mahat*)—great
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—unique (one without a second)

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

People, we proclaim and praise the fact that Indra, the hero, is endowed with horses. The gods too know that Indra is endowed with horses. The horses, which are of the nature of time as the six seasons, are five in form through the union of the seasons Hemanta and Śiśira, and they carry Indra. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
We proclaim, people, the wealth of the hero, (Indra), in horses ; the gods know his (affluence) ; six, or five and five, harnessed to his car, convey him ; great and unequalled is the might of the gods,

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

षोळ्ता (*ṣoḷtā*)—मासानां द्वंद्वयोगकाले षोढा दृश्यमानाः ऋतवः अश्वाः निरूप्यंते । (*māsānāṃ dvaṃdvayogakāle ṣoḍhā dṛśyamānāḥ ṛtavaḥ aśvāḥ nirūpyaṃte |*) । ते च षट् संख्याकाः (*te ca ṣaṭ saṃkhyākāḥ*) । ऋतवः हेमंतशिशिरयोः समासेन पंचपंच युक्ताः संतः कालात्मकमिंद्रं आवहंति । (*ṛtavaḥ hemaṃtaśiśirayoḥ samāsena paṃcapaṃca yuktāḥ saṃtaḥ kālātmakamiṃdraṃ āvahaṃti |*) । तदिदं इंद्रस्य स्वश्वत्वं यदृतभिरूढत्वं (*tadidaṃ iṃdrasya svaśvatvaṃ yadṛtabhirūḍhatvaṃ*) ।
It is described that Indra is endowed with excellent horses, and that the gods too know this endowment of Indra with excellent horses: अस्य स्वश्वत्वं देवा आपि जानंति (*asya svaśvatvaṃ devā āpi jānaṃti*). The endowment with excellent horses stated here is explained by the exposition "ṣoḷhā". Indra is of the form of time; for Indra, who is of the nature of time, the twelve months combine into six pairs of seasons. Of these, if the two seasons Hemanta and Śiśira join as one, there are five seasons. Thus these seasons, five in number, are represented as five horses; these five horses carry Indra, who is of the form of time. This is what is meant by Indra's being endowed with excellent horses through the seasons. Although six seasons arise from twelve months, Hemanta and Śiśira, being possessed of one and the same kind of quality, are reckoned as one. Thus the five seasons are five horses, and they carry Indra, who is time-natured through identity with the sun; and the greatness of Indra is described as mighty.
वीरो वीरयत्यमित्रान् वेतेर्वा स्याद्गतिकर्मणः वीरयेतेर्वा (*vīro vīrayatyamitrān vetervā syādgatikarmaṇaḥ vīrayetervā*) (Ni. 1-7). Yāska explains the word vīra thus: one who destroys enemies in many ways, who goes to face the enemies and confronts them, who is endowed with valour.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The verse is the anuvākyā for the oblation in the Tvāṣṭra animal sacrifice, the verse देवस्त त्वष्टेतेषा (*devasta tvaṣṭeteṣā*); and it is prescribed in the sūtra (Ā. Sū. 3-8).**NOTE** Savitā is the impeller of all as the inner controller; Tvaṣṭṛ, the god so named, of many kinds of form (viśvarūpa), begets the creatures in many ways (purudhā) and nourishes them. All these worlds, all the beings, belong to this Tvaṣṭṛ.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- सविता (*savitā*)—the impeller of all
- विश्वरूपः (*viśvarūpaḥ*)—the one with many kinds of form
- त्वष्टा देवः (*tvaṣṭā devaḥ*)—Tvaṣṭṛ, who is of divine nature
- प्रजाः (*prajāḥ*)—the creatures
- पुरुधा (*purudhā*)—in many ways
- जजान (*jajāna*)—creates
- पुपोष (*pupoṣa*)—(and) nourishes
- इमा विश्वा भुवनानि (*imā viśvā bhuvanāni*)—all these beings, all of them
- अस्य (*asya*)—belong to this Tvaṣṭṛ
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods
- असुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ*)—the might
- महत् (*mahat*)—great
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—extraordinary

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Tvaṣṭṛ, the impeller of all, of many kinds of form, of divine nature, creates the creatures in many ways and nourishes them. All these beings too belong to that Tvaṣṭṛ. The might of the gods is great and extraordinary.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
The divine Twashtri the impeller (of all), the multiform, has begotten and nourished a numerous progeny, for all these worlds are of him : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

### Printed p. 314

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

सविता (*savitā*)—अंतर्यामितया सर्वस्य प्रेरकः (*aṃtaryāmitayā sarvasya prerakaḥ*) । Sāyaṇa explains that the word savitṛ means "one who impels everything, since he is the inner controller". Yāska explains: सविता सर्वस्य प्रसविता (*savitā sarvasya prasavitā*)—Savitā is the one who brings forth everything.
त्वष्टा देवः प्रजाः पुरुधा जजान पुपोष विश्वा भुवनानि च अस्य (*tvaṣṭā devaḥ prajāḥ purudhā jajāna pupoṣa viśvā bhuvanāni ca asya*)—तृष्णनामकः देवः प्रजाः बहुधा जनयति पोषयति (*tṛṣṇanāmakaḥ devaḥ prajāḥ bahudhā janayati poṣayati*) । इमानि सर्वाणि भूतजातानि च त्वष्टुः संबंधीनि (*imāni sarvāṇi bhūtajātāni ca tvaṣṭuḥ saṃbaṃdhīni*) । Sāyaṇa states that the god named Tvaṣṭṛ has fashioned the creatures in many ways and nourishes them, and that all these creatures belong to the god Tvaṣṭṛ.
Yāska gives the etymology of this Ṛk as follows: देवस्त्वष्टा सविता सर्वरूपः पोषति प्रजाः रसानुप्रदादेन बहुधा चेमा जनयतीमानि च सर्वाणि भूतान्वयदकान्यस्य महच्चास्मै देवानामसुरत्वमेकं प्रज्ञावत्त्वं वानवत्त्वं नापि ना । (*devastvaṣṭā savitā sarvarūpaḥ poṣati prajāḥ rasānupradādena bahudhā cemā janayatīmāni ca sarvāṇi bhūtānvayadakānyasya mahaccāsmai devānāmasuratvamekaṃ prajñāvattvaṃ vānavattvaṃ nāpi nā |*) । असुरिति प्रज्ञानाम अस्यत्यनर्थान् अस्ताश्चास्यामर्थाः (*asuriti prajñānāma asyatyanarthān astāścāsyāmarthāḥ*) । असुरत्वमादिलुप्तं (*asuratvamādiluptaṃ*) । (Ni. 10-34) The god Tvaṣṭṛ has brought all creatures into being. By bestowing waters he nourishes and increases them. These beings and the waters belong to this god; therefore this god produces the creatures, nourishes and increases them. Hence the asuratva of this god is explained as extraordinary. He also explains the meaning of the word asura: because it averts dangers, nothing is expressible by the word asu as "intelligence", or falls outside the range of intelligence; therefore asura is said to mean "possessed of intelligence".**NOTE** And: असुरत्वं वसुमतो भावः वसुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ vasumato bhāvaḥ vasuratvaṃ*) । रः मत्त्वर्थे वकारलोपश्च (*raḥ mattvarthe vakāralopaśca*) वसुना उदकेन तद्वान् असौ त्वष्टा (*vasunā udakena tadvān asau tvaṣṭā*) । He explains that the word asuratva is used for vasuratva, that here "ra" is used in the sense of "possessing" and that "va" is dropped, and he gives another meaning: वसुना उदकेन तद्वान् (*vasunā udakena tadvān*)—one who is endowed with waters. Durgācārya comments: तया महत्या प्रज्ञया उदकेन साधनेन सर्वमिदं जनयति पुष्णाति वर्धयति च । (*tayā mahatyā prajñayā udakena sādhanena sarvamidaṃ janayati puṣṇāti vardhayati ca |*)—being possessed of abundant intelligence, the god Tvaṣṭṛ produces everything by means of the waters, nourishes it and increases it. In the second explanation given by him: असुरत्वं अन्नवत्त्वं (*asuratvaṃ annavattvaṃ*) । असुः प्राणः तेन तद्वत्वं (*asuḥ prāṇaḥ tena tadvatvaṃ*)—asuratva is the state of being endowed with breath; अन्नवत्त्वं तेषामन्नहेतुनोदकेन तद्वत्वं (*annavattvaṃ teṣāmannahetunodakena tadvatvaṃ*)—he is endowed with the waters that are the cause of food for the creatures.

### Printed p. 315
In Sāyaṇa's explanation, विश्वा भुवनानि (*viśvā bhuvanāni*) is given the meaning सर्वाणि भूतजातानि (*sarvāṇi bhūtajātāni*)—the totality of creatures of many kinds. In the Nirukta commentators' explanation, सर्वाणि भूतानि उदकानि (*sarvāṇi bhūtāni udakāni*)—he makes all creatures and the waters, nourishes and increases them; thus a difference can be seen. A difference is also seen in the explanation of the meaning of the word asuratva.

> मही समैरच्चम्वा समीची उभे ते अस्य वसुना नृष्टे ।
> शृण्वे वीरो विंदमानो वसूनि महद्देवानामसुरत्वमेकं ॥ २० ॥

> अस्य । वसुना । नृष्टे इति निऋष्टे ।
> शृण्वे । वीरः । विंदमानः । वसूनि । महत् । देवानां । असुरत्वं । एकं ॥ २० ॥

> *mahī samairaccamvā samīcī ubhe te asya vasunā nṛṣṭe |*
> *śṛṇve vīro viṃdamāno vasūni mahaddevānāmasuratvamekaṃ ‖ 20 ‖*
> *mahī iti | sam | airat | camyā | samīcī iti samīcī | ubhe iti | te iti |*
> *asya | vasunā | nṛṣṭe iti niṛṣṭe |*
> *śṛṇve | vīraḥ | viṃdamānaḥ | vasūni | mahat | devānāṃ | asuratvaṃ | ekaṃ ‖ 20 ‖*
> मही महत्वा समीचि परस्परं संगते चम्वा चमंत्यदंत्यनयोर्देवमनुष्या इति चम्वौ । यद्वा चम्येते आद्येते भूतजातैरिति चम्वौ द्यावापृथिव्यौ ।
> समैरत् । इंद्रः प्रजापश्वादिभिः सम्यगयोजयत् । ते उभे द्यावापृथिव्यावस्येंद्रस्य वसुना तेजसा धनेन वा नृष्टे निकरां व्याप्ते भवतः।वीरः समर्थः स इंद्रो
> वसूनि शत्रूनभिभूय तदीयानि धनानि विंदमानो लभमानः सन् श्वण्वे । सर्वैः
> श्रूयते । तवेदिदमभितश्चेकिते वसु। ऋग्वे. १-५३-३ । इत्यादिषु दृष्टत्वात् ॥ ऐरत्।
> ईर गतावित्यस्य लजि रूपं । नृष्टे । ऋषी गतौ । कर्मणि क्तः । गतिरनंतर इति गतेः
> स्वरः । शृण्वे । श्रु श्रवण इत्यस्य व्यत्ययेन कर्मणि श्नुः । लोपस्त आत्मनेपदेष्टिति
> तलोपः । विंदमानः । विद्ल लाभ इत्यस्य लटि शानचि रूपं । तस्य लसार्वधातुकस्वरे
> धातुस्वरः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

चम्वा (*camvā*) (dual) are the two that are "chewed", for in them gods and men eat (चमंत्यदंत्यनयोर्देवमनुष्या इति (*camaṃtyadaṃtyanayordevamanuṣyā iti*)); or else they are the two that are eaten by the creatures—heaven and earth. "Mahī" means great, "samīcī" mutually joined. समैरत् (*samairat*): Indra joined them well with creatures, animals and the rest. Both heaven and earth are pervaded by this Indra's वसुना (*vasunā*)—by his splendour or by his wealth. वीरः (*vīraḥ*) means capable. That Indra, overcoming his enemies and obtaining their wealth (वसूनि (*vasūni*)), is heard of by all; for this is seen in such passages as तवेदिदमभितश्चेकिते वसु (*tavedidamabhitaścekite vasu*) (Ṛgve. 1-53-3).**NOTE**

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मही (*mahī*)—those of great nature
- समीची (*samīcī*)—and joined together
- चम्वा (*camvā*)—heaven and earth
- सम्मैरत् (*sammairat*)—(Indra) made them endowed with creatures
- ते उभे (*te ubhe*)—both of them, heaven and earth
- अस्य (*asya*)—of Indra
- वसुना (*vasunā*)—by the splendour
- नृष्टे (*nṛṣṭe*)—are pervaded
- वीरः (*vīraḥ*)—the capable Indra
- वसूनि (*vasūni*)—the wealth of enemies
- विंदमानः (*viṃdamānaḥ*)—as one who seizes
- शृण्वे (*śṛṇve*)—is heard of as well known
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods
- असुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ*)—the might
- महत् (*mahat*)—great
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—unique

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Indra made heaven and earth, which are of great nature and joined together, endowed with creatures. Both heaven and earth are pervaded by Indra's splendour. It is well known that Indra, the capable, seizes the wealth of enemies. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
He has filled the two vast receptacles (heaven and earth) united (with creatures): they are both penetrated by his lustre: the hero spoiling the treasures (of the foe) is renowned : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

चम्वा (*camvā*)—चमंति अदंति अनयोः देवमनुष्याः इति चम्वा (*camaṃti adaṃti anayoḥ devamanuṣyāḥ iti camvā*) । यद्वा चम्येते अद्येते भूतजात्यैरिति चम्वा द्यावापृथिव्यौ । (*yadvā camyete adyete bhūtajātyairiti camvā dyāvāpṛthivyau |*) । The word chamvā is stated among the names of heaven and earth (Ni. 3-22). Since they are the cause of the production of food fit to be eaten by gods and men, and since they are consumed by all creatures, heaven and earth are designated by the word chamvā.
वसुना (*vasunā*)—तेजसा धनेन वा (*tejasā dhanena vā*) । The word vasu is stated among the names of rays (Ni. 2-15) and among the names of wealth (Ni. 3-9); and in सुगुर सत्सुहिरण्यः (*sugura satsuhiraṇyaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-1-18) it is used in the sense वसुना अन्नेन (*vasunā annena*)—"with food". And it is also explained: वसवः आदित्यरश्मयः (*vasavaḥ ādityaraśmayaḥ*) (Ni. 12-42)—the rays of the sun. Here it is described that heaven and earth are pervaded by Indra's splendours and wealth, pervaded by Indra's lordliness.

### Printed p. 317
वीरः वसूनि विंदमानः शृण्वे (*vīraḥ vasūni viṃdamānaḥ śṛṇve*)—समर्थः सः इंद्रः शत्रूनभिभूय तदीयानि धनानि लभमानस्सर् (*samarthaḥ saḥ iṃdraḥ śatrūnabhibhūya tadīyāni dhanāni labhamānassar*) सर्वैः श्रूयते (*sarvaiḥ śrūyate*)**NOTE**—having explained that the heroic Indra subdues his enemies and seizes their wealth, he describes that this matter is stated in the Ṛk तवेदिदमभितश्चेकिते वसु (*tavedidamabhitaścekite vasu*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-53-3).

> इमां च नः पृथिवीं विश्वधायाउप क्षेति हितमित्रो न राजा।
> इमां । च । नः । पृथिवीं । विश्वधायाः । उप । क्षेति । हितमित्रः ! न ! राजा ।
> पुरःसदः । शर्मसदः । न । वीराः । महत् । देवानां । असुरत्वं । एकं ॥ २१ ॥

> *imāṃ ca naḥ pṛthivīṃ viśvadhāyāupa kṣeti hitamitro na rājā|*
> *imāṃ | ca | naḥ | pṛthivīṃ | viśvadhāyāḥ | upa | kṣeti | hitamitraḥ ! na ! rājā |*
> *puraḥsadaḥ | śarmasadaḥ | na | vīrāḥ | mahat | devānāṃ | asuratvaṃ | ekaṃ ‖ 21 ‖*
> विश्वधाया विश्वस्य धाता सर्वान्नो ना नोऽस्माकं राजेंद्र इमां पृथिवीमंतरिक्षं चोप तयोः समीपे क्षेति । निवसति । तत्र दृष्टांतः । हितमित्रो न । यथा
> कस्यचित् हितोपदेष्टा सुहृत्समीपे निवसति तद्वत् । वीराः समर्था युद्धसहाया
> मरुतः पुरःसदो युद्धार्थं पुरतो निश्चयेन गंतार इंद्रस्य शर्मसदः । न
> चार्थे । शर्मणि गृहे सीदंतश्च भवंति । यत्र यत्रासौ तत्र तत्र संनिधिं कुर्वाणा
> इत्यर्थः ॥ क्षेति । क्षि निवासगत्योरित्यस्य लटि बहुलं छंदसीति विकरणस्य लुक् । निघातः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

विश्वधायाः (*viśvadhāyāḥ*) is the supporter of all. Our king Indra dwells near this earth and the atmosphere, close to them. The illustration: हितमित्रो न (*hitamitro na*)—as a friend who gives beneficial counsel dwells near one's side. The वीराः (*vīrāḥ*) are the capable Maruts, helpers in battle, पुरःसदः (*puraḥsadaḥ*)—those who go resolutely before Indra for battle; शर्मसदः (*śarmasadaḥ*)—here न (*na*) is in the sense of "and" (न चार्थे (*na cārthe*)): they are also seated in his house (śarman); the meaning is that wherever he is, there they keep close at hand.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- विश्वधायाः (*viśvadhāyāḥ*)—the supporter of the whole world
- नः (*naḥ*)—to us
- राजा (*rājā*)—the lord, Indra
- हितमित्रो न (*hitamitro na*)—like a friend who wishes one well
- इमां पृथिवीं उप (*imāṃ pṛthivīṃ upa*)—in the atmosphere near this earth
- क्षेति (*kṣeti*)—dwells
- वीराः (*vīrāḥ*)—the capable Maruts
- पुरःसदः (*puraḥsadaḥ*)—going in front of him (in battle)
- शर्मसदः (*śarmasadaḥ*)—dwell in his very house
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods
- असुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ*)—the might
- महत् (*mahat*)—great
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—extraordinary

### Printed p. 318

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Indra, the supporter of the whole world and our lord, dwells like a friend who wishes us well in the firmament nearest to this earth. The valiant Maruts go in front of him in battle and dwell in his own house. The might of the gods is great and unequalled.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Our king, the nourisher of all, abides (in the firmament) nearest to this earth like a benevolent friend : the valiant (Maruts) precede him (when abroad), and dwell in his mansion : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

विश्वध्वायाः नः राजा इमां पृथिवीं च उप क्षेति (*viśvadhvāyāḥ naḥ rājā imāṃ pṛthivīṃ ca upa kṣeti*): the meaning is explained as follows. Indra, who supports and nourishes the whole universe, or who enjoys everything, is king and protector for us, the sacrificers, and dwells close to earth and the firmament. For this, the illustration हितमित्रो न (*hitamitro na*) is given: just as a friend who counsels one's welfare always lives nearby, so Indra, staying near earth and the firmament, is described as one who thinks of our good.

वीराः (*vīrāḥ*): the able Maruts, helpers in battle. Although the word "vīra" is conventionally used in the sense of "hero", here it is used in the sense that the Marut deities are heroes and help Indra in times of battle.

पुरसदः शर्मसदो न (*purasadaḥ śarmasado na*): these Maruts are those who go in front of Indra in battle and who also dwell in Indra's house; they are present wherever he is. The meaning is explained thus: the Maruts stay in front of Indra and help in times of battle, and they dwell in all the places where Indra is. The particle "na" is stated to have the sense of comparison and also the sense of prohibition (Ni. 1-4); here that particle is given the sense of the particle "ca", that of combination.

> सर्वॆ वननीयधनभागिनो भवेम । तदेतद्देवानां महदैश्वर्यं ॥ निष्पिध्वरीः ।
> षिधु संरादौ । संपदादिलक्षणो भावे क्विप् । तदस्यास्तित्यर्थे छंदसीवनिपाविति
> वनिप् । वनो र चेति जीप् रेफश्च । निसा सह समासः । निसः सकारं छांदसत्वादनादृत्योपसर्गात्सुनोतीत्यादिना षत्वं । जीपः पित्त्वा दनुदात्तत्वे धातुस्करः । बिभर्ति।
> डुभृञ् धारणपोषणयोरित्यस्य लटि बृञामिदित्यभ्यासस्यॆत्वं । निघातः । वामभाजः । भज सेवायां । भजो ण्वैः । पा ३-२-६२ । इति ण्वैः । कृदुत्तरपदस्वरः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

O Indra, in the form of Parjanya (the rain-god): the plants (ओषधीः (*oṣadhīḥ*)) are निष्पिध्वरीः (*niṣpidhvarīḥ*), that is, brought fully to perfection through you; and the waters also flow forth from you. The earth bears for you wealth fit for your enjoyment; Sāyaṇa cites the Nigama "Earth bears abundant treasures" (Ṛgve. 3-51-5). Therefore we, your friends and praisers who help you with offerings, would be वामभाजः (*vāmabhājaḥ*), sharers of all desirable wealth. That is the great lordship of the gods. **NOTE**

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra, who are of the nature of Parjanya
- ओषधीः (*oṣadhīḥ*)—all the plants also
- ते (*te*)—by you alone
- निष्पिध्वरीः (*niṣpidhvarīḥ*)—obtain nourishment and fullness of sap
- उत (*uta*)—and
- आपः (*āpaḥ*)—the waters also flow forth from you alone
- पृथिवी (*pṛthivī*)—the earth
- ते (*te*)—for you
- रयिं (*rayiṃ*)—wealth
- बिभर्ति (*bibharti*)—has borne
- ते (*te*)—to you
- सखायः (*sakhāyaḥ*)—we, who are your friends
- नामभाजः स्याम (*nāmabhājaḥ syāma*)—may we enjoy all these riches **NOTE**
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods
- असुरत्वं (*asuratvaṃ*)—the might
- महत् (*mahat*)—is great
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—and unique

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, of the nature of Parjanya, all the plants also receive nourishment and fullness of sap from you alone. The waters flow forth from you alone. The earth has borne wealth for you. May we, your friends, enjoy all this wealth. The might of the gods is great and unique. **NOTE**

### Printed p. 320

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
The plants, Indra, come to perfection by you : from you the waters (flow) ; earth bears her treasures for you : may we, your friends, be sharers of these blessings : great and unequalled is the might of the gods.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

Addressing him with the word Indra, it is described that Indra, being the giver of rain to the worlds, performs the acts of producing, nourishing and increasing everything, and is therefore of the nature of Parjanya.

सखायः वामभाजः स्याम (*sakhāyaḥ vāmabhājaḥ syāma*): we, the helpers and praisers by the offering of oblations, would all be sharers of desirable wealth. It is described that the sacrificers wish Indra's welfare by offering oblations to him and by praising him; it is further explained that these sacrificers hope to obtain from Indra the wealth that is necessary for performing sacrifices and the like, and that the great might of the gods is chief and unequalled.

Closing verse and colophon: वेदार्थस्य प्रकाशेन तमो हार्दं निवारयन् । पुमर्थांश्च तुरो देयाद्विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरः ॥ (*vedārthasya prakāśena tamo hārdaṃ nivārayan | pumarthāṃśca turo deyādvidyātīrthamaheśvaraḥ ‖*) इति श्रीमद्राजाधिराजपरमेश्वरवैदिकमार्गप्रवर्तकश्रीवीरबुक्क भूपालसाम्राज्यधुरंधरेण सायणाचार्येण विरचिते माधवीये वेदार्थप्रकाशे ऋक्संहिताभाष्ये तृतीयाष्टके तृतीयोऽध्यायः समाप्तः (*iti śrīmadrājādhirājaparameśvaravaidikamārgapravartakaśrīvīrabukka bhūpālasāmrājyadhuraṃdhareṇa sāyaṇācāryeṇa viracite mādhavīye vedārthaprakāśe ṛksaṃhitābhāṣye tṛtīyāṣṭake tṛtīyo 'dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ*) यदक्षरपदभ्रष्टं मात्राहीनं तु यद्भवेत् । तत्सर्वं क्षम्यता० देव वागीश्वर नमोऽस्तु ते (*yadakṣarapadabhraṣṭaṃ mātrāhīnaṃ tu yadbhavet | tatsarvaṃ kṣamyatā0 deva vāgīśvara namo 'stu te*) May there be auspiciousness. Blessing. ओं तस्यत् (*oṃ tasyat*). Here ends the third chapter in the third Aṣṭaka of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, with the bhāṣya of Śrī Sāyaṇa and the Kannada translation.

Om. Śrī. Obeisance to the great lord of the troops. वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानामुपक्रमे यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युस्तं नमामि गजाननं ॥ (*vāgīśādyāḥ sumanasaḥ sarvārthānāmupakrame yaṃ natvā kṛtakṛtyāḥ syustaṃ namāmi gajānanaṃ ‖*) यस्य निश्यसितं वेदा यो वेदेभ्योऽखिलं जगत् । निर्ममे तमहं वंदे विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरं ॥ (*yasya niśyasitaṃ vedā yo vedebhyo 'khilaṃ jagat | nirmame tamahaṃ vaṃde vidyātīrthamaheśvaraṃ ‖*) तृतीयाष्टकमध्यस्थः तृतीयोऽध्याय आदरात् । व्याख्यातः सायणार्यॆण चतुर्थो व्याकरिष्यते ॥ (*tṛtīyāṣṭakamadhyasthaḥ tṛtīyo 'dhyāya ādarāt | vyākhyātaḥ sāyaṇāryèṇa caturtho vyākariṣyate ‖*) वेदः शिवः शिवो वेदो वेदाध्यायी सदाशिवः । तस्मात्सर्वप्रयत्नेन वेदमेव सदा जपेत् ॥ (*vedaḥ śivaḥ śivo vedo vedādhyāyī sadāśivaḥ | tasmātsarvaprayatnena vedameva sadā japet ‖*)

Ṛgveda Saṃhitā with the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya. The fourth chapter in the third Aṣṭaka. (Sūktas 56-62 of the third Maṇḍala and Sūktas 1-4 of the fourth Maṇḍala.)

In this chapter, beginning with the 56th Sūkta of the third Maṇḍala, the third Maṇḍala ends with the 62nd Sūkta. Although the Viśvedevas are the deity of this Sūkta, the Āditya, the year and its divisions are praised. Because in many places there are no words indicating a definite meaning, and because room is left for many kinds of meanings, it is not possible to say that the seer's intention for many of the matters stated in this Sūkta is just so. Nevertheless, following the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, we have given the explanation of the meaning in accordance with Yāska's etymologies.

## Sūkta 56 (Maṇḍala 3)
The fifty-sixth Sūkta.

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> न ता मिनंतीत्यष्टर्चं तृतीयं सूक्तं विश्वामित्रस्य वाचः पुत्रस्य ना प्रजापतेरार्षं त्रैष्टुभं वैश्वदेवं । तथा चानुक्रमणिका । न ताष्टाविति। सूक्तविनियोगो
> लिंगादवगंतव्यः । अस्मिन्सूक्ते प्रायेणादित्यैः सह संवत्सरः स्तूयते ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The hymn beginning न ता मिनंति (*na tā minaṃti*), of eight ṛks, is the third sūkta. Its seer is Prajāpati, the son of Viśvāmitra, or Vācya, son of Vāc; the metre is Triṣṭubh and the deity the Viśvedevas. The Anukramaṇikā says न ताष्टाविति (*na tāṣṭāviti*). The use of the sūkta in ritual is to be understood from the indication (liṅga) of its content. In this sūkta, for the most part, the year is praised together with the Ādityas.

Anuvāda: This Sūkta beginning "na tā minanti" is the third Sūkta in the fifth anuvāka. It has eight ṛks. Its seer is Prajāpati or Vācya, the son of Viśvāmitra; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the metre is Triṣṭubh. The Anukramaṇikā says "na tāṣṭau". The use of the Sūkta is to be understood according to the meaning of the ṛks. In this Sūkta the year is for the most part praised together with the Āditya.

Om. Sūkta 56. Maṇḍala 3; Anuvāka 5; Sūkta 56. Aṣṭaka 3; Adhyāya 4; Varga 1. Number of ṛks in the Sūkta: 8. Seer: Prajāpati Vaiśvāmitra or Vācya. Deity: the Viśvedevas. Metre: Triṣṭubh.

> न । रोदसी इति । अद्रुहा । वेद्याभिः । न । पर्वताः । निनमे । तसि ऽवांसः ॥ १ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> मायिनः कपटबुद्धुपेता असुरा देवानामिंद्रादीनां प्रथमा प्रथमानि
> सृष्ट्यनंतरभावीनि ध्रुवाणि स्थिराणि केनापि चालयितुमशक्यानि ता तानि लोके
> प्रसिद्धानि व्रता व्रतानि लोकपालनादिकर्माणि न मिनंति । न हिंसंति । तथा धीरा
> विद्वांसोऽपि न हिंसंति । तथाद्रुहा देवमनुष्यादिषु प्रजासु द्रोहवर्जिते
> रोदसी द्यावापृथिव्य वेद्याभिः स्वाश्रयतया सर्वैर्वेदनीयाभिः प्रजाभिः सहितानि
> कर्माणि न मिनीतः । तदेतदुपपादयति । तस्थिवांसः पृथिव्यामूर्ध्वतया स्थिताः
> पर्वता न निनमे । निनमनीया न भवंति । एतदुक्तं भवति । यद्देवमनुष्यादीनां
> द्यावापृथिव्याधारकतयावस्थापनं यच्च पर्वतादीनामुन्नततयावस्थापनं तदिदं
> देवानां कर्म । तन्न कोऽप्यन्यथयितुमर्हतीति ॥ मिनंति । मीज् हिंसायामित्यस्य
> लटि मीनातेर्निगम इति ह्रस्वः । निघातः । वेद्याभिः । वेदनमर्हंति । छंदसि चेति
> यत्पत्ययः । निनमे । णमु प्रह्वत्व इत्यस्य कृत्यार्थे केन्प्रत्ययः । कृत्स्वरः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The मायिनः (*māyinaḥ*) are the asuras, endowed with a deceitful mind. The acts (व्रता (*vratā*)) of the gods, Indra and the rest, that is, the works such as protecting the world, are प्रथमा (*prathamā*), coming first after creation, and ध्रुवाणि (*dhruvāṇi*), firm, impossible for anyone to move, and well known in the world. These the asuras do not मिनंति (*minaṃti*), that is, do not injure; likewise the wise (धीरा (*dhīrā*)) do not injure them. Likewise रोदसी (*rodasī*), heaven and earth, free from hostility (अद्रुहा (*adruhā*)) toward the beings of gods, men and the rest, do not injure the works together with the beings, वेद्याभिः (*vedyābhiḥ*), who are known to all through their dependence on them. He substantiates this: the mountains (पर्वता (*parvatā*)) standing (तस्थिवांसः (*tasthivāṃsaḥ*)) high on the earth are not निनमे (*niname*), they are not to be bowed down. What is meant: the establishing of gods, men and the rest as the supporters of heaven and earth, and the setting up of mountains and the like as lofty, are the works of the gods; no one is able to alter them.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मायिनः (*māyinaḥ*)—the deceitful asuras
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—of the gods, Indra and others
- प्रथमा (*prathamā*)—most ancient and chief
- ध्रुवाणि (*dhruvāṇi*)—firm
- ता (*tā*)—and well-known
- व्रता (*vratā*)—acts such as protecting the world
- न मिनंति (*na minaṃti*)—cannot injure and obstruct
- धीराः (*dhīrāḥ*)—even the wise and discerning
- न (मिनंति) (*na (minaṃti)*)—cannot injure
- अद्रुहा (*adruhā*)—free from hostility
- रोदसी (*rodasī*)—heaven and earth also
- वेद्याभिः (*vedyābhiḥ*)—together with their communities of beings, evident to all
- न (मिनीतः) (*na (minītaḥ)*)—cannot injure
- तस्थिवांसः (*tasthivāṃsaḥ*)—firmly established
- पर्वताः (*parvatāḥ*)—mountains
- न निनमे (*na niname*)—(because they are established by Indra and the others) no one can lower their loftiness

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Neither the deceitful asuras nor the wise and discerning can injure and obstruct the most ancient, firm and well-known acts of the gods, such as protecting the world. Even heaven and earth, free from hostility, cannot obstruct them. The loftiness of the mountains and the like, set high upon the earth, is also the work of Indra and the others, so no one can lower them.

### Printed p. 324

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Neither the deceptive nor the resolute interrupt the primitive and permanent operations of the gods, nor do the innocuous heaven and earth (interrupt them), nor are the mountains standing (on the earth) to be bowed down.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

The power of the works of Indra and the others, such as protecting the world, is the matter of this mantra. The affairs of the universe go on in accordance with the law of the seasons (ṛtu-dharma). All activities that proceed in conformity with and in support of this rule are called vrata. The breaking of this vrata of Indra and the others cannot be effected by anyone. However deceitful and powerful the asuras may be, they cannot break these vratas. The wise and steadfast follow this same vrata, so no breach arises from them either. Therefore the affairs of the universe proceed in order just as was resolved before creation; thus the steadiness of the cosmic order is praised.

The cosmic order can be broken by two kinds of power. It may be attempted by demonic power, which hates divine culture and acts with deceit to gain selfish ends. Or poets who are filled with divine power itself, who are wise, and who can independently produce creation in accordance with Brahma's creation, may be able to break it. But there is ample basis for saying that in the affairs of the universe divine power has greater strength than demonic power. Therefore the breaking of the vrata of Indra and the others is not possible for the asuras or persons with demonic power; and since the steadfast poets and the wise have resolved to promote divine culture itself, they too cannot break this law. This is what is suggested in this mantra.

मायिनः (*māyinaḥ*): this word is explained as the asuras endowed with a deceitful mind. The word māyā is used in many places in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā to denote an extraordinary special power. There are contexts in which it also means an independent creative power. The epithet here denotes the creative power of the gods Indra and the others. Therefore, to understand the purport of the word in the present place, one must know in what contexts the word is used elsewhere in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā.

Broadly it can be said that this word is used in four main senses: as divine creative power, as merely physical power, as stratagem, or as the art of magic (indrajāla). It can be said to be derived from the root माज् माने (*māj māne*) **NOTE**, which has the sense of creation.

### Printed p. 325
"Māyā means prajñā (intelligence)": मायेति प्रज्ञानाम । माया, वयुनं इति तन्नामसु पाठात् । (नि. ३-१३) (*māyeti prajñānāma | māyā, vayunaṃ iti tannāmasu pāṭhāt | (ni. 3-13)*) Thus the Nirukta-writers have explained this word as prajñā. Citing the Ṛks मायामू तु यज्ञियानां (*māyāmū tu yajñiyānāṃ*) (10-88-6) and शुक्रं ते अन्यद्यजतं ते (*śukraṃ te anyadyajataṃ te*) (6-58-1), the appropriateness of taking the word as prajñā there was explained earlier (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Part 11, p. 514).

रूपंरूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव तदस्य रूपं प्रतिचक्षणाय । इंद्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश ॥ (*rūpaṃrūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tadasya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya | iṃdro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hyasya harayaḥ śatā daśa ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-18)

This well-known mantra describes Indra's power of māyā. It is also recited in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. Sāyaṇa explains this mantra in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā in two ways. First: मायाभिः—ज्ञानमेतत् । ज्ञानैः । आत्मीयैः संकल्पैः (*māyābhiḥ—jñānametat | jñānaiḥ | ātmīyaiḥ saṃkalpaiḥ*)—by cognitions that are of the nature of his own resolves Indra took on manifold forms. Second: इदि परमैश्वरै इत्यस्य धातोरर्थानुगमात् इंद्रः परमात्मा । स चाकाशवत् सर्वगतः सदानंदरूपः (*idi paramaiśvarai ityasya dhātorarthānugamāt iṃdraḥ paramātmā | sa cākāśavat sarvagataḥ sadānaṃdarūpaḥ*)—the word Indra is formed from the root id, which gives the sense "lord of the whole universe"; therefore Indra here means the Supreme Self. He explains that the all-pervading Supreme Person is transformed, by his powers of māyā, into the form of the world beginning with ether. In both constructions the word māyā is taken as creative power. Moreover, Śaṅkarācārya too explains this mantra in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka in two ways: first प्रज्ञाभिः (*prajñābhiḥ*), by intelligences that effect creation; second नामरूपभूतकृतमिथ्याभिमानैर्वा (*nāmarūpabhūtakṛtamithyābhimānairvā*), that is, by powers of imagining such as "I" and "form". Here too the purport of the word is creative power. Power of imagination means mental creation. Mental creation may lack physical reality, but creative power must be present. For both kinds of power the synonym māyā is used in many places. Likewise:

माया वां मित्रावरुणा दिवि श्रिता सूरो ज्योतिश्चरति चित्रमायुधं । तमभ्रेण वृष्ट्या गूहथो दिवि पर्जन्य द्रप्सा मधुमंत ईरते ॥ (*māyā vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā divi śritā sūro jyotiścarati citramāyudhaṃ | tamabhreṇa vṛṣṭyā gūhatho divi parjanya drapsā madhumaṃta īrate ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-63-4)

In all such places the extraordinary intelligence and creative power of Mitra and Varuṇa are described. Likewise, in the previously cited mantras such as मही मित्रस्य वरुण्य माया (*mahī mitrasya varuṇya māyā*) there is no room for the sense "ignorance" for māyā. In पूर्वापरं चरतो माययौता (*pūrvāparaṃ carato māyayautā*) (10-85-18) it is said that the Sun and Moon travel in the atmosphere by their special power of intelligence; there is no imagination in this, it is physical truth. Therefore, as stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya and the like,

### Printed p. 326
there is no room for the sense of ignorance or imagination. This meaning becomes clear if one examines the mantra cited in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa in the Pravargya section:

पतंगमक्तमसुरस्य मायया हृदा पश्यंति मनसा विपश्चितः । समुद्रे अंतः कवयो वि चक्षते मॆरीचीनां पदमिच्छंति वेधसः (*pataṃgamaktamasurasya māyayā hṛdā paśyaṃti manasā vipaścitaḥ | samudre aṃtaḥ kavayo vi cakṣate mèrīcīnāṃ padamicchaṃti vedhasaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-177-1)

There Sāyaṇa explains the word asura as the Supreme Brahman and māyā as the intelligence belonging to the Supreme Brahman. Pataṅga means the Sun. The wise realise, with the heart and a restrained mind, that is, in meditation, the Sun pervaded (aktaḥ) by the intelligence of the Supreme Brahman. Hence here too there is no room for "ignorance". Just as in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā the resolve of Indra and others is designated by the synonym māyā, so the Gītā too follows it; to show this, in the Śrī-bhāṣya, in the Antaradhikaraṇa, the Gītā sentence प्रकृतिं स्वामधिष्ठाय संभवाम्यात्ममायया (*prakṛtiṃ svāmadhiṣṭhāya saṃbhavāmyātmamāyayā*) (Bha. Gī. 4-6) is cited and the word māyā there is explained as intelligence in the form of the Lord's resolve. The Nirukta sentence माया वयुनं, ज्ञानं (*māyā vayunaṃ, jñānaṃ*) is recited there as authority. There is no need to explain here what the exact purport is of the word māyā in the Brahma-sūtra passage माया मात्रं.... (*māyā mātraṃ....*) and the like, nor what the source of the māyā-doctrine is in philosophical procedure, its essential meaning, how this idea grew, or the purport of the contradictory statements.

Besides creative resolve or power, the word is also used in the senses of deceit, fraud, trickery:

त्वं मायाभिरनवद्य मायिनं श्रवस्यता मनसा वृत्रमर्दयः । त्वामिन्नरो वृणते गविष्टषु त्वां विश्वासु हव्यास्विष्टिषु ॥ (*tvaṃ māyābhiranavadya māyinaṃ śravasyatā manasā vṛtramardayaḥ | tvāminnaro vṛṇate gaviṣṭaṣu tvāṃ viśvāsu havyāsviṣṭiṣu ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-147-2)

Here both meanings of the word māyā are shown: the intelligent Indra destroyed the deceitful enemy. Therefore, when used of Indra and the other deities, the word means creative resolve or powerful intelligence; when used of the asuras, it means deceit or fraud. In the present Ṛk too the word is used in the sense of power. Deceitful asuras need extraordinary power to obstruct the guardian and other works of the gods. But the vrata of the gods, protectors of ṛta, is not to be broken by anyone.

Vratā: the word vrata is explained as works such as protecting the world. The meaning of the word is an act performed under a fixed rule. From this point of view, in general the word vrata

### Printed p. 327
is well known as the name for sacrifices and other rites that humans perform for the gods, to please them. Here, however, the word vrata is used for the works of Indra and others; in the present Ṛk the works of the gods are also called vrata. That is, such usages show that, as the performance of sacrifice is necessary for a human from the Vedic point of view, so works such as protecting the world are equally necessary for the gods.

In sentences such as अग्ने व्रतपते व्रतं चरिष्यामि (*agne vratapate vrataṃ cariṣyāmi*) (Śa. Brā. 1-1-1-2) the common relation of gods and humans to vrata is indicated. Vrata can be taken to mean yajña. But if one asks how to say which of the works a human does is yajña and which is not, one must examine a mantra in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā as the answer:

नानानं वा उ नो धियो वि व्रतानि जनानां । तक्षा रिष्टं रुतं भिषग्ब्रह्मा सुन्वंतमिच्छतींद्रायेंदो परि स्रव ॥ (*nānānaṃ vā u no dhiyo vi vratāni janānāṃ | takṣā riṣṭaṃ rutaṃ bhiṣagbrahmā sunvaṃtamicchatīṃdrāyeṃdo pari srava ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-112-1)

In this mantra the many-sided works of humans are described. The vratas of people are many. Among them, the carpenter wishes to do carpentry, the physician to treat disease, the sacrificer to press soma and perform the sacrifice. That is, if each person does the occupation suited to his capacity and nature, with faith and from a sense of duty, then all the works of a human are in the form of vrata; the very life of a human is in the form of vrata. In the same way all the works that the gods do for the maintenance of the world are vrata. As a human performs sacrifices and the like for the gods' satisfaction, the gods too must supply the wealth of help suited to the human's existence and nourishment. This discharge of duty is described here as vrata. As firm as all the vratas observed according to the law of the seasons are the vratas of the gods.

Two explanations of the word vrata are given in the Nirukta: निवृत्तिकर्म वारयतीति सतः (*nivṛttikarma vārayatīti sataḥ*)—since it forbids improper actions, it is called vrata; or since it chooses the duty to be done, it is called vrata (वृणोतीति सतः (*vṛṇotīti sataḥ*) Ni. 2-12). In the explanation वृणोतीति व्रतं (*vṛṇotīti vrataṃ*) the duty that every individual, human or god, must observe regularly is indicated. Third: यदावृणोति शरीरं । तस्मादन्नमपि व्रतमुच्यते (*yadāvṛṇoti śarīraṃ | tasmādannamapi vratamucyate*) (Ni. 2-12). Because it pervades the whole body and gives it strength, food too is called vrata. The word vrata in the present Ṛk can be taken to mean food. The purport is that since the wealth of food supplied by the gods is firm, no one can harm it.

### Printed p. 328
Dhīrāḥ: धीरो धीमान् (*dhīro dhīmān*)—this word is read among the names of the intelligent (Ni. 3-9). In the Vedas and Upaniṣads the word is used in the sense of wise, discriminating. Since the dhīra is wise, and has qualities such as conquering fear and being fearless, remaining calm of mind even in calamity, the purport is "courageous". Citing sentences such as महांतं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति (*mahāṃtaṃ vibhumātmānaṃ matvā dhīro na śocati*) (Kaṭha 5-4)**NOTE**, the distinctive character of this word was explained earlier. Since the wise, discerning person follows the vrata of the gods, there is no violation of this cosmic order. For deceitful asuras it is not possible. Therefore the vratas of the gods are unshakable and eternal. The vrata of Varuṇa, described in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā as dhṛtavrata, is likewise described elsewhere. The nature of these vratas, which cause the world's stability and protection, is this:

अमी य ऋक्षा निहितास उच्चा नक्तं ददृश्रे कुह चिद्दिवेयुः । अदब्धानि वरुणस्य व्रतानि विचाकशच्चंद्रमा नक्तमेति ॥ (*amī ya ṛkṣā nihitāsa uccā naktaṃ dadṛśre kuha ciddiveyuḥ | adabdhāni varuṇasya vratāni vicākaśaccaṃdramā naktameti ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-24-10)

The light of the stars at night and the light of the sun by day are Varuṇa's vratas. The rule of this vrata is unobstructed. Varuṇa's command is the command of the universe; no one can transgress it. Because of this inviolability Mitra and Varuṇa are described as dhṛtavrata (Ni. 8-25-2)**NOTE**. Likewise:

नहि त्वा शूर देवा न मर्तासो दित्संतं । भीमं न गां वारयंते ॥ (*nahi tvā śūra devā na martāso ditsaṃtaṃ | bhīmaṃ na gāṃ vārayaṃte ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-8-3)

Neither gods nor humans can hinder the great, generous works of Indra. All Indra's works are in the form of vrata; therefore the purport is that they are firm and protect the world.
